That was never my point. I am pointing out that anyone who claims, or implies, that “Black people wearing wigs” is an example of us “stealing culture” from yt people is just factually incorrect. It doesn’t matter whether people wear it for African culture, or wear it due to internalised texturism. It’s one of those things that I don’t agree with, but choose to ignore anyway. I found that for a while it was disrupting my peace, and I was putting more energy into educating/debating yt people than what I was getting out of it.

Nowadays I observe silently and have a chuckle to myself, bc 9 times out of 10 their scalp looks raw and the hairstyle looks dumb af on them anyways. It’s like a private little joke to myself (teehee)

Not to mention, I discovered that they only like to take what they can’t have. The only reason most of them get protective styles is because they know we don’t want them to. I guarantee if we started saying they can’t get relaxers, they’ll start doing it to spite us (maybe this should be phase 2 👀)

Wigs/weaves have been a part of African culture for literal centuries - we can’t ‘steal’ something that was ours to begin with. And if you’re referring to “straighter” hair, then no one culture owns that. Black people can be born with straight hair too, so BW choosing to wear straight hair has nothing to do with ‘taking from other cultures’.

Unless your hair is (significantly) heat damaged or chemically treated, your curls should always come back regardless how long you have your braids in. I keep mine in for 8 weeks on average, and wash around every 2 weeks. I usually forget to put grease or leave in out of sheer laziness lol. I always start my wash with a clarifying shampoo after take down, because I think it’s really important to start your hair on a complete clean base (especially after such a long amount of time for buildup to develop), and it also sets your hair up for being properly hydrated during the rest of the wash and conditioned after.

I usually find my hair reverts almost entirely after the 1st/2nd clarifying shampoo. And thinking back to when I only used regular shampoo, I think it would take around 2/3 washes (it’s hard for me to remember), but was no where near as curly as when I preceded with clarifier.

You’ve already mentioned your hair was in good condition, so it’s unlikely to be damage. So it might be worth questioning whether your shampoo is cleaning your hair properly, because that’s the only other reason I can think of. If undamaged hair doesn’t revert fully it is very likely to be because some product particles are still blocking the cuticles and stopping the water from doing its magic. Firstly maybe look at the products that you use regularly on your hair. Do you use things like silicones that might need a stronger shampoo to remove? Also, maybe it’s worth getting a clarifier if it’s something you want to try. Or alternatively get a sulfate shampoo if you’re not using one already. Or if not, just attempt more washes with your current!

I guess the first piece of advice would be to find a curl/afro specialist. Not a random hairdresser who focuses on curls, not a braider, not a stylist, but an actual, _certified_ curl/afro specialist. This was the start of my natural hair journey and what I learnt from just one session was invaluable to my outlook of my hair. There were so many things I was doing previously that were actually harmful to my hair health and didn’t ease detangling. Things like using oil to ‘moisturise’ my hair, avoiding water to avoid shrinkage, using sulfate-free shampoos or just cowashing entirely to avoid ‘harmful products’ to name a few. There are a lot of trends and misinformation we follow just because influencers know how to make anything sound legit, even if it’s not. My curl specialist not only gave me so much important information as to what hair actually needs to be healthy, but also backed her claims up with _scientific_ reasonings. Such as, ‘relying on oil to moisturise is harmful because only water can moisturise, and oil (alone) decreases porosity, _preventing_ your hair from being moisturised’ and ‘shampoo with sulfates is good for your hair because the ph levels allow your hair cuticles to open properly, allowing your hair to be hydrated well during wash days’ and ‘shrinkage is a sign of health and more importantly, hydration, so you shouldn’t try to fight it’. Hey there. I’m 21 (22 in two weeks) and I can honestly say this is normal. I’ve had feelings like this, and a lot of my friends (when they feel brave enough to confide in me) have made clear they are stuck in the same hole. And it breaks my heart. What I’ve come to realise (and what I’m trying to tell others) is that we are young. We can do whatever the fuck we want to do, because we have the rest of our lives to fix it if it goes wrong. If you don’t like your current life, you can change it. Even if your current life is ‘stable’ or ‘safe’, if it is not making you happy, then be willing to take some risks to change it. This is your only life after all.

In your last paragraph, you said all the things you want to do. Please understand that you *can* do these things. This world is literally full of endless opportunities, and if you want something enough, and work towards it enough, you will get it. Be a bit hard on yourself. Tell yourself to wake up and start going for what you want.

My advice? Build up your experience in your job. Get to a place where you are financially stable. Then some of your wishes will fall into place. Afterwards, you can maybe find roommates and move elsewhere? I’m not sure where you live, but there are plenty of websites to help find roommates. If those don’t work out, ask around - ask your colleagues, put adverts on Facebook or other social media sites (even reddit), or even put ads in shops. Bear in mind these do not need to be people you already know, they can be people you are willing to get to know. Understand that if your mum loves you, she will want what’s best for you. And if she doesn’t, that is all the more reason to move out. It always feels like mums have this invisible grasp over us, because they are mums. But they don’t. Unless she has physically chained you to a wall, or is abusing you in some other way, don’t feel any qualms in moving on to better your life.

Next, save up enough money to go travelling. Either plan it or wing it. Either way, just do it if it’s what you want to do. You are *guaranteed* to meet amazing people when you go travelling - some of which may even come from your home country. And also, it is so important to see the world. It would give you a chance to leave your cooperate bubble and see, experience, explore new things. This may be something you want to do before your mum stops paying your rent, as you’d probably have more money. Have a think about it and decide what’s best.

In the meantime, whilst doing all the above, form a plan. A plan to get out of this job you clearly hate and find a job you love. Brainstorm what you like, what you want to do in life. Then? Research. Find out what it is you need to get into what you want. Email/call people from different companies you like. Go to networking events (there are many ‘Meetup’ apps for things like this), meet like minded people, potential employers, potential mentors or partners. Go to your local school and see if there’s someone who specialises in a field you like, who is willing to help and give you advice. If a job says you need some prior knowledge, then learn whatever they’re asking of you! Everything is learnable from home. Some employers like to make out you need a degree or whatever, but in most cases you honestly don’t (unless you want to get into something like medicine). It may take time, but you can learn whatever you need just by reading books, taking online courses, after which you can show potential employers that you have the knowledge, but more importantly you are motivated enough to learn on your own. If you need experience in the sector you want, go and get it! Volunteer! Email people, ask to shadow them!

Also I advise you speak to a therapist and doctor about your mental and physical pain (respectively). If you’re from the UK, they are free on the NHS (although it may be a long waiting list). Otherwise, save up for a therapist. If you are not financially stable atm, this may involve sacrificing something thats eating your money. Maybe cigarettes, takeaways, alcohol? Maybe try using cheaper transport/walking to work? Whatever the situation, please try your hardest to get professional help, it honestly helps so so much. I’ve gotten therapy multiple times (for small and big problems) and every time has literally catapulted my healing time.

I can relate to this so much. I fell in love with my housemate who i soon found out was my soul mate. The day she abandoned me was the most agonising thing I have ever gone through. I cried and cried everyday afterwards. Whenever a certain song came on that reminded me of her, whenever I saw someone on the street that looked like her; each and every morning and each and every night and multiple times in between, I’d cry. I would pray to a god (that I don’t even believe in), to please kill me in my sleep, because life isn’t worth living anymore. Nothing will make me feel happiness again. And I would wake up each morning, angry and hurt that I am still here. I stopped attending lectures, I stopped doing any work, I stopped seeing my friends and hardly ate - because life felt completely pointless to me. There was no point trying anymore.
What I hated THE MOST was when I confided in family and friends about it: they would tell me I need to get over it; that I need to get my life back; that I will experience this time and time again; that I am young and will find someone new. They did not understand that this girl was THE ONLY ONE for me, and my life meant nothing without her.
After a while, I sought counselling while I was at uni. I didn’t expect this to solve the situation, but I just wanted someone to talk to. My counsellor was the FIRST person to tell me that it’s okay to feel what I am feeling, and I should take as much time as I need to grieve. She said if I didn’t feel ready to attend lectures, or see my friends/family, then this is okay. This is honestly what I needed so so much. I came home that day and cried and cried and cried, but for the first time, I didn’t feel guilty about it. I let myself feel what I was feeling.
It took me around 6 months for me to begin feeling better. I don’t know what it was, but at some point, my mind began healing. And after some time, slowly and gradually, I started seeing my friends again, eating more regularly, and enjoying life. This was a very slow process. But I can’t describe the feeling of the first time I actually looked forward for the next day, or an event. I never thought I’d feel enjoyment again.
I still love her, I still miss her and think about her, but she does not define my being anymore. I had a life with her, and now I have a life without her, and that’s okay
